body_markdown:
Porsche 911 fans are a difficult bunch to please. They love their chosen sports car, yet any significant update is met with deep suspicion. Recall the hoo-ha surrounding the 1997 launch of the 996 generation that brought in a water-cooled engine to meet ever more stringent emission regulations. By the reaction, you’d think Porsche had dropped in an engine from a tractor (or, as with a previous Porsche,[a van…](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/the-porsche-924-wasnt-born-a-porsche-it-became-one-revelations-with-jason-cammisa/) ). So it should come as no surprise that a similar type of nose-up reaction greeted the 964 when it launched in 1989, as this 911 was no less radical in the updates and improvements it ushered in.


The 964’s development began in earnest in 1986, with design work by Benjamin Dimson. His reshuffling of the classic 911 shape was sympathetic to the model it was set to replace, and a cursory glance suggests it was little more than a new set of bumpers.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


However, 87% of the 964 was all-new, and the more you looked, the more you spotted what was different, redesigned, and just plain better than on the outgoing car. Among the biggest changes was the new M64 flat-six engine, which made 247 horsepower from its 3.6 liters. There was also all-wheel drive for the first time and a Tiptronic automatic gearbox, plus coil-spring suspension.


While the purists sat and fumed at these changes, Porsche got on with launching the 964 to the public, beginning with the Carrera 4 coupe, with its all-wheel drive, five-speed manual gearbox, and that air-cooled flat-six. The car featured power steering, anti-lock brakes, and twin front airbags, which made the 964 heavier than the Carrera 3.2 it replaced, but the 33 extra ponies of its engine compensated. A 964 Carrera 4 coupe could cover 0–60 mph in 5.6 seconds and hit 162 mph.


It was the same for the Carrera 2 when it arrived in 1990, along with the Targa and Cabriolet models. The new Tiptronic four-speed automatic gearbox was only available on the rear-drive Carrera 2 and dulled performance slightly, so the sprint to 60 mph took 6.2 seconds, while top speed dipped to 159 mph.


Hagerty Marketplace/JohnTerranova_gxsn


Hagerty Marketplace/MiamiGarageClassics


You could have your 964 open as a Targa (left) and even more open as a Cabriolet.


From there on, Porsche was on a roll with new versions of the 964. The rear-drive, 320-hp Turbo arrived in 1991, with power from the old 3.3-liter Type 930 engine, along with distinctive, broad rear arches and trademark whale tail. Porsche ironed out the kinks of turbocharging the M64, and in 1993 introduced a 3.6-liter Turbo with 355 hp. In between there was a lightweight 3.3 Turbo S and later a 3.6 Turbo S, along with some *flachbau* slant-nose versions, with styling that hinted at the forthcoming 993 generation.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


The first 964 Turbos (left) utilized the previous generation’s 3.3-liter engine, while later Turbos featured the 3.6.


If you were so inclined, you could order a standard C2 coupe or Cabriolet with the Turbo-look body style, and in 1992 Porsche reintroduced the RS badge to its 911 range, with a lightweight, homologation-special for Europe. Like its illustrious predecessors, the new RS came with thinner window glass, a stripped interior, a tuned engine, and a lower, stiffer suspension. Revised gearing made the most of the RS’s power, which provided 0–60mph in 5.1 seconds and an identical 162-mph top end to the Carrera 2. More important, however, was how the RS went around corners, which it did brilliantly. To comply with U.S. safety regulations, a less sporting variant was made in 1993–94, aptly named the RS America. It was based on the Carrera 2 and shed some 77 pounds but lacked the cutting edge of its Euro counterpart. An RS 3.8 in 1993 swapped the narrow-hipped body for that of the Turbo, while also squeezing out a cool 300 horses.


Broad Arrow


After a five year-absence, in 1994 Porsche also reintroduced the Speedster to the 911 range. With its cut-down windscreen, it gave the impression of being all about performance, but underneath it was stock Carrera 2 fare.


And then it was all over for the 964. The car enjoyed a brief five-year lifespan before it was replaced by the final air-cooled model, the 993.


## What’s a 964 Like to Drive?


Broad Arrow


If you’re expecting the 964 to feel similar to 911s of the past 25 years, you’re in for a shock. It’s not just the different noise and feel of the air-cooled engine that grabs your attention, but the cars’ far more visceral sensations—and that’s just in standard C2 or C4 configurations. Even with its greatly improved coil-spring suspension, the 964 has a firm ride quality that’s less refined than a later 911. This also translates to more road noise at higher speeds.


The payoff, however, is that the 964 has an immediacy of response to any steering or throttle input that you just don’t get in later generations of 911. In many ways, it’s the ideal balance between that classic 911 feel and modern mechanical robustness. Sure, the nose still bobs up and down on bumpy roads, but it remains planted in corners, and the rear end won’t try to kick out at the merest hint of throttle lift-off mid-corner.


All of this means that rapid cross-country driving in a 964 is a real pleasure, and the sometimes-derided all-wheel-drive C4 offers superb traction in all conditions. Even so, the C2 is the more rewarding driver’s car, and the five-speed manual gearbox has a light, slightly notchy shift. A Tiptronic auto can feel sluggish in its changes compared to a modern transmission, but it works well when you adjust your thought processes to the period technology.


Broad Arrow


As with all 911s, the flat-six accounts for a great deal of the experience, and the 964’s air-cooled motors are delightful. On paper, and by modern standards, the 247-hp 3.6 doesn’t sound that potent, but it has oodles of low- and mid-rev torque, followed by a howling top end. Again, it’s less refined than later 911s, but it’s also a joy to listen to. As for the Turbo, there’s a definite lag as it spools up, so care is needed to drive it accordingly. If given the opportunity to experience an RS, you’ll find the suspension almost too firm for road use, but it is fantastic for point-to-point blasts.


Inside, the 964 is built to Porsche’s typically high standards of the period. You can also find cars with air conditioning to make coupes more usable during summer. The switchgear is not as scattered as in previous 911s, with five main dials in the cluster and the rest of the controls for heating and stereo grouped close to the driver on the central dash. All-round vision is excellent thanks to the slim pillars and surprisingly upright windscreen.


Settle into the front seats and they might seem a little thin on padding at first, but they are supportive and comfortable. However, this 911 is quite narrow, so space for elbows and hips can be limited when there’s a front passenger aboard. And don’t bother trying to fit anyone into the rear seats; just use them as extra storage in addition to the small front trunk.


## How Much Does a 964 Cost?


Broad Arrow


There are clear strata in the 964 model range, delineated by body type, transmission, and engine. Starting with the Carrera 2 and 4,[near-perfect coupes](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1991/1991-porsche-911-carrera_2?id=aCn1I000000CyzESAS&condition=concours) in #1 (concours) condition are now approaching[the $200K mark](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1991/1991-porsche-911-carrera_4?id=aCn1I000000CvPvSAK&condition=concours) , with the slightest bump in the C2’s favor. Those in #2 (excellent) shape are closer to the $135K–$160K range, while competent drivers in #3 (good) condition are roughly $90K–$125K. If you’re shopping for a C2 or C4 Cabriolet, you can knock off a big chunk of value from the coupes:[around $100K less](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1991/1991-porsche-911-carrera_2?id=aCn1I000000DFlUSAW) than their top-end pricing,[$50K less](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1991/1991-porsche-911-carrera_4?id=aCn1I000000DFGJSA4) than the excellent ones, and about $30K–$40K less than the good ones. Targas, however,[are valued a lot closer](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1991/1991-porsche-911-carrera_2?id=aCn1I000000D9ZOSA0&condition=excellent) to their fixed-roof counterparts,[no matter the condition](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1991/1991-porsche-911-carrera_4?id=aCn1I000000CxcxSAC&condition=excellent) . For all C2 and C4 964s, buyers put a premium on those with manual transmissions, so Tiptronic cars tend to come with a 10% discount.


In the 964 forced-induction sphere, the best 3.3-liter Turbos can now command $400,000, with excellent examples around $270K–$325K, and[well-loved drivers](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1992/1992-porsche-911-turbo?id=aCn1I000000DGEzSAO) in the neighborhood of $180K–$235K. The 3.3-liter Turbo S is exceptionally rare, with just 86 built, and it is priced accordingly.[The best ones](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1992/1992-porsche-911-turbo_s?id=aCn1I000000DUKSSA4) are $1.0–$1.3M cars, while excellent cars top out at the million-dollar mark and good ones hover in the $550K–$700K range. The later 3.6-liter Turbos are more appealing in the market, and values across the board are[roughly double](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1994/1994-porsche-911-carrera_turbo?id=aCn1I000000Cs7uSAC&condition=excellent) their 3.3 counterparts in similar condition.


The RS America, while not as razor-sharp as its European cousin (now[a half-](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1992/1992-porsche-911-carrera_rs?id=aCn1I000000DBMrSAO)[million](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1992/1992-porsche-911-carrera_rs?id=aCn1I000000DBMrSAO)[-dollar machine](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1992/1992-porsche-911-carrera_rs?id=aCn1I000000DBMrSAO) in the right condition), still commands a premium over standard Carrera 2, with the very best[priced from $270K–$330K](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1994/1994-porsche-911-rs_america?id=aCn1I000000CrL4SAK) and good drivers exactly half that. Finally, if you fancy an open 964 but want something different,[Speedsters can be had](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/1994/1994-porsche-911-carrera?id=aCn1I000000CrX1SAK&condition=concours) for $175K–$225K in good shape and $355K–$435K in concours shape.


## What to Look for When Buying a 964


Stefan LombaBroad Arrowrd


The 964 languished at the cheap end of the 911’s price scale for a long time, so you want to be on the lookout for signs of neglect and/or poor restoration work. And given Porsche’s reputation for build quality, it also might surprise you to know the first thing to look for on any 964 is rust.


Start at the front with the headlamp surrounds and where the fenders meet the bumper, then check all around the windshield and rear window. Inspect all over the rear arches and the inner arches where the suspension mounts are. If all of these areas are sound, the rest of the body should be in good condition.


Hagerty Marketplace/MiamiGarageClassics


An entire Cabriolet roof is expensive to replace at around $3000–$5000 all in, but the plastic rear window can be swapped for mere hundreds. The motors that clamp the soft-top to the windscreen rail can break and can cost several hundred bucks to rebuild. Also check the interior for any signs of moisture in the Cabrio or Targa models, as seals go brittle with age and will need to be replaced. The interior of the 964 is generally hard-wearing, so you just need to make sure it’s all there and in good order. If the car has air conditioning, expect it to need a service at some point, as it was never the most effective even when new.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Hagerty Marketplace/KMSibH


Broad Arrow


Moving on to the engine, the M64 unit is a tough customer and will easily cover 100,000 miles without a problem if serviced according to schedule. The most likely issue to arise is broken cylinder head studs, which will show up with leaks or a high-speed misfire, and a full rebuild of both cylinder heads can creep into five figures. Cars from 1991 on had an improved gasket where the head meets the block, which solved the earlier engine’s tendency to leak oil from here.


Broad Arrow


Porsche used a dual-mass flywheel for the 964’s manual gearbox, and earlier versions up to 1992 are more prone to failure. This will be obvious by a rattle and vibration as the engine idles. Later cars had an improved LUK dual-mass flywheel, and most of the earlier Freudenberg versions should have been replaced by now unless you find a very low-mileage car.


Lastly, look for a car that has had a distributor vent kit fitted. This helps prevent the failure of the distributor belt, which can lead to terminal engine damage if it breaks. Also, don’t be put off by a 964 that has had some engine or suspension upgrades, so long as they are backed up by documentation to show that an acknowledged specialist performed the work.


## Which Is the Right 964 for You?


Broad Arrow


Most buyers in the market for a Porsche 964 will already know which body style and drivetrain they want. The Cabriolet, Targa, and rarer Speedster offer open-air cruising, but they are not quite the driver’s cars that a coupe is. This helps explain why coupes are more expensive to buy; demand is simply higher. It also shows why a good C2 with the manual gearbox typically achieves higher prices; it’s the most sought-after model for good reason. Of all the standard 964s, this is the one to have.


However, don’t be put off by a Carrera 4, as the all-wheel-drive system is not intrusive, and it offers excellent traction in the wet and winter. The Tiptronic four-speed automatic gearbox is more of a personal choice, but it is a good bet if you spend a good deal of time driving in a city.


The more exotic 964 versions will always have their fans, and Turbo 3.6 cars are highly prized for good reason. The 3.3 Turbo is not quite as venerated, which makes it a bit of a bargain for a car that is still thrilling to drive. However, for some it’s the RS America that will be the one to own, with its weight savings over a standard C2 and resulting sharper performance.
